title: Boeing Lands $131B F-15 'Eagle Crest' Contract as F-35 Lifecycle Cost Dips Below $2 Trillion
subhead: The US Air Force sole-sourced a $131.2 billion ceiling contract to Boeing for F-15 production and sustainment through 2037, while a new Pentagon report pegs F-35 total lifecycle cost at $1.93 trillion. Japan approved mass production of 3D-printed interceptor drones and the US Army moved to buy 8,000 short-range missiles a year.

sections.heading: Boeing's $131B F-15 'Eagle Crest' Contract
sections.body: The US Air Force awarded Boeing a sole-sourced, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract worth up to $131.2 billion for the F-15 fighter, according to a Defense Department announcement reported by Breaking Defense. The 'Eagle Crest' vehicle covers aircraft production, upgrades and sustainment for the Pentagon and international F-15 customers, with work expected to run through August 2037. An Air Force spokesperson stressed the ceiling 'represents capacity for future needs, not a commitment to spend the full amount.' Casey Nicastro of the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments called it 'one of the bigger contracts recently awarded' by the Pentagon.
sections.whyItMatters: The F-15, a 1970s-era airframe, is being locked in as a long-term workhorse alongside the F-35 — a signal that the Air Force is betting on a high-low fighter mix and keeping Boeing's St. Louis line alive for another decade-plus.

sections.heading: F-35 Lifecycle Cost Dips Below $2 Trillion
sections.body: A Pentagon selected acquisition report covering 2025, reported by Breaking Defense, now estimates the F-35 will cost about $536.3 billion to acquire all planned tri-variant copies — up from $485.2 billion in the 2024 report. But total lifecycle cost, including operations, is projected at roughly $1.93 trillion, slightly below the $2.06 trillion estimate from 2024. The acquisition-cost rise reflects higher procurement prices even as the overall program estimate fell.
sections.whyItMatters: The F-35 remains the most expensive weapons program in history, and the divergence — rising buy costs but a lower lifecycle total — points to a smaller or differently-phased fleet than originally planned.

sections.heading: Japan Approves Mass Production of 3D-Printed Interceptor Drones
sections.body: Japan's Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency signed a mass-production agreement for the Terra B1, a rocket-launched interceptor drone developed by domestic firm Terra Drone, Defense News reported. The B1, selected after a demonstration with the Maritime Self-Defense Force, is the Japan-made counterpart to the Terra A1 fielded in Ukraine. ATLA did not disclose order numbers or price, but the move is part of Tokyo's push to rapidly deploy a large unmanned fleet by 2027 to counter one-way attack drones.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is industrializing cheap, 3D-printed counter-drone interceptors — a model tested on Ukraine's battlefields — reflecting how the drone-defense market is shifting toward mass, low-cost production.

sections.heading: US Army Seeks 8,000 Short-Range Missiles a Year
sections.body: The US Army issued a Sources Sought notice for a Hellfire/Joint Air-to-Ground Missile-class weapon, seeking up to 8,000 new short-range missiles per year, Defense News reported. The missile must integrate with manned and unmanned air, ground and waterborne platforms using an M299 launcher, with a range of 500 to 8,000 meters, and target heavy armor, air-defense radars, counter-UAS and small fast-attack maritime craft. Responses are due Sept. 15.
sections.whyItMatters: The volume — 8,000 a year — shows the Army is scaling up precision-strike production dramatically as it rebuilds munitions stocks depleted by the Iran and Ukraine conflicts.

sections.heading: Nordic Counter-Drone Cooperation and EU Defense Financing
sections.body: Finland and Sweden agreed to strengthen military cooperation by enhancing Helsinki's counter-drone capabilities amid recent aerial incursions, Breaking Defense reported, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen framing it as cooperation on 'territorial surveillance and protection of territorial integrity' on NATO's eastern flank. Separately, Italy requested €8 billion ($9.3 billion) in cheap loans from the EU's SAFE defense program, Defense News reported, scaling back an earlier, larger request.
sections.whyItMatters: Both moves reflect the post-2022 European defense buildout: Nordic states hardening against drone incursions near Russia, and EU members tapping Brussels' SAFE facility to fund rearmament.

sections.heading: Non-Western Defense: UAE-Brazil Cyber Center and India's Engine Contest
sections.body: Emirati conglomerate EDGE Group launched a Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence with the Brazilian army — the first of its kind in South America, Breaking Defense reported — operating under a tripartite government-industry-academia model. In India, Rolls-Royce and Safran are competing to co-develop a 120 kN-class engine for the AMCA Mk-2 stealth fighter, Defense News reported, with Rolls-Royce partnering Reliance Industries on a proposed aerospace gas-turbine complex and Safran offering full technology transfer with DRDO.
sections.whyItMatters: Gulf and South American defense ties are deepening beyond traditional Western supply chains, while India's push for an indigenous fighter engine targets its single biggest aerospace vulnerability.

bottomLine: The US defense industrial base is locking in long-term production commitments — Boeing's $131B F-15 ceiling and the Army's 8,000-missiles-a-year requirement — even as the F-35's lifecycle estimate edges below $2 trillion. Japan's move to mass-produce 3D-printed interceptor drones and the Nordic counter-drone push show the drone-defense market maturing toward cheap, scalable production. Meanwhile, UAE-Brazil and India's engine contest signal that defense-industrial cooperation is diversifying beyond the traditional Western axis.
sources: Breaking Defense, Defense News, Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments (via Breaking Defense)
